newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh stocks seen depressed until February.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh stocks seen depressed until February.

text.p: Investors in Bangladesh's securities market have blamed the government for the recent erratic market which saw a steep rise and a near-crash, and analysts see stocks remaining depressed until February.
The government has formed a committee to determine why share prices have moved so dramatically.
The share price fall triggered unrest in the kerb market and led to the shutdown of Bangladesh's main Dhaka Stock Exchange (DSE) for two days this month.
The DSE benchmark index that shot up to 3,648.74 on November 5 in euphoric trading by thousands of retail investors fell to 2,618.3 on December 7. The Index was as low as 1,145.54 on August 1.
"The government intervention is to be blamed for the recent fall in the market," said broker Syed Tareque M. Ali.
He said the government was wrong to set a price fluctuation limit last month. "The government wanted to curb the unbridled price hike, but instead it backfired," he told Reuters.
Ali said the market was now uncertain. "I don't know where the market is heading to."
He said the market was likely to remain depressed until February. "It normally remains a bit slow during the year-end period and in the Ramadan month (January-February)," he said.
Former DSE chairman Khurshid Alam said the huge kerb market and repeated government interventions were responsible for destabilising the stock market.
He said the government's failure to meet the mounting demand by retail investors pushed prices abnormally high and the market had overheated.
"I believe the market will continue to remain unstable against this backdrop," he said.
Broker Abdur Rashid said: "The rise in the past had no relation to company fundamentals. It has to come down.

"I think the index should come down to the 1,600-1,800 level. It may hurt many investors, but at the same time one should realise that the prices must have some relativity to company earnings," he said.
Finance Minister S.A.M.S. Kibria acknowledged there had been a setback in the country's capital market.
"We have had rather an unhappy experience in the stock market," he told Reuters in a recent interview.

"No one should expect that the price of the shares will double every week and that there will be a windfall. I think this kind of expectation is artificial and unrealistic, and it has misled many people," he said.
Kibria said the government would soon set up a national stock exchange "in order to rectify some of the deficiencies of the stock exchange".
